newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. and Japan firms move back to S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: U.S. and Japan firms move back to S.Africa.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese companies, traditionally the most cautious of foreign investors, are slowly returning to South Africa after shunning the country during the apartheid era.

Among U.S. players, General Motors Corp. is the latest edging closer to a return to South Africa after Delta Motor Corp., which has 9 percent of the local car market, said it was discussing closer links with the car giant.
Industry sources said another well-known U.S. concern would also announce a major investment next week.
Meanwhile, Japan's Nissan Motor. confirmed Friday what the local market has suspected for weeks, that it could take a stake running into hundreds of millions of rand in South Africa's Automakers Ltd.

Two other Japanese concerns, Komatsu Ltd and Itochu Corp., also said they were investing 90 million rand ($20 million) in a construction equipment joint venture with Anglo American Industrial Corp. Ltd.

David Perlstein, head partner or corporate finance at Ernst & Young in Johannesburg, said there was a widespread rekindling of interest in direct investment in South Africa, although many companies were still cautious.

"There hasn't been a flood from anywhere -- we're seeing fairly constant across-the-board interest," he said. "For example, we've been getting enquiries from Canadians recently, which is something we haven't seen for a long time."

Direct inward foreign investment into South Africa jumped from 820 million rand ($179 million) in 1994 to 3.7 billion rand ($810 million) in 1995, following the first all-race elections in April 1994.

Last year the figure is likely to have topped 4.0 billion rand ($875 million), according to Trade and Industry Minister Alec Erwin, who said in an interview earlier this week that investment had increased some seven to eight percent in 1996.
To date, American and Japanese companies have been more wary than those from other countries about investing in South African bricks and mortar.
But that could be changing, according to Erhard van de Merwe, director of corporate finance at Coopers and Lybrand.

"The Americans have been cautious so far, but as long as others like the French, British, Germans and, particularly, the Malaysians increase their investment, they won't want to be left behind," he said.

The latest major U.S. company to return to South Africa was Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co., which bought 60 percent of local tiremaker Contred for $121 million, including assumed debt, in a deal with Anglovaal Industries Ltd last November.
Other recent returnees include industrial group Owens Corning and drugs group American Home Products.
Nissan's interest in Automakers follows Toyota Motor Corp.'s decision to pay 446 million rand ($98 million) for a 28 percent stake in Toyota South Africa last October.
The biggest outside investment in South Africa so far is Malaysian oil company Petronas' 1.9 billion rand ($416 million) investment in Engen Ltd last year.

But that should be topped soon with the government's planned sale of up to 30 percent of telecommunications group Telkom by April. That deal, expected to value Telkom at over $4 billion will be sub-Saharan Africa's biggest privatisation yet.
Two consortia are in the running, with Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom pitched against SBC Communications and Telekom Malaysia.
